edition.note: Expanded edition: new desks for courts and regulators, shadow markets, deals and earnings, and a country-by-country roundup. Indian prices are from mid-morning Mumbai trade.

lead.headline: Anthropic Prices a Record $81 Billion IPO and Debuts Today
lead.dek: Shares priced at $83, above the range, value the AI developer near $1.5 trillion; Nasdaq futures climb about 1% into the first trade.
body: Anthropic set its offering price at $83 a share on Wednesday evening, US time, above the $70 to $78 range it had marketed. Selling 980 million shares, it raised about $81 billion, the largest initial public offering on record and bigger than SpaceX's. At that price the company is worth roughly $1.5 trillion on a fully diluted basis, up from $965 billion in its last private round in May. Trading on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT starts on Thursday.

Alongside the listing, a group of chip and cloud partners, AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia and a TSMC affiliate, agreed to buy $26 billion of non-voting shares in a private placement. Amazon owns close to 15% of the company and Google about 14%, according to the filing, and each of the seven co-founders, including chief executive Dario Amodei, is selling about $282 million of stock.

The pricing landed on a nervous day. The Dow lost 561 points as health insurers collapsed and the Fed's October minutes pointed to more rate hikes, and the S&P 500 slipped below its 200-day moving average for a fifth straight loss. Yet the Nasdaq rose 0.42%, carried by companies tied to the deal: Amazon gained 3.8%, AMD 5.3% and Broadcom 3.6%.

Overnight, Nasdaq-100 futures were up about 1% and S&P 500 futures about 0.6% in Asian hours. Demand above the range suggests investors are still willing to pay for AI growth even after November's rout in chip and software stocks, though the size of the deal also pulls a large amount of cash toward a single new name.

impact.title: What it means for markets
points: Direct winners are the shareholders and partners: Amazon and Alphabet hold large stakes that are now marked to a public price, and AMD, Broadcom, Micron and Nvidia gain a deep-pocketed customer with fresh capital.
A strong first day would support the broader AI and IPO pipeline; a weak one after an above-range pricing would revive November's doubts about AI valuations.
Index funds cannot buy yet, so early trading is driven by active money. Watch whether buying ANT is funded by selling other megacap tech.

highlights.text: Anthropic prices at $83, raising about $81 billion in the biggest IPO ever; ANT starts trading on Nasdaq today.
Fed minutes: almost all officials expect further hikes; Waller floats a half-point move in December and the dollar hits a 19-month high.
Health insurers crash on a proposed Medicare Advantage audit rule: Humana -13%, UnitedHealth -10%, dragging the Dow down 561 points.
Gold sinks 3.5% to about $3,729, its lowest since September 2025, as silver and copper tumble about 5%.
Trump, Xi and Putin sit down in Shenzhen today for the first three-way leaders' meeting, with Iran, Ukraine and trade on the table.
Washington weighs wider strikes on Iran as a loaded tanker is hit in Hormuz; Brent briefly tops $93.
Europe falls for a third day: DAX -1.2%, FTSE 100 -1.3% as miners slump; euro-area inflation is confirmed at 4.0%.
Taiwan's Taiex crashes 4.4% below 39,000 and regulators curb short selling; Kospi closes up 1.4%.
EU blacklists 113 more shadow-fleet operators; India's grey market cools on the Mahanadi Coalfields IPO.
UK inflation rises to 3.6%; Brazil's real hits a six-month low; Bank Indonesia hikes to 6%.
Indian stocks steady after Wednesday's slide; autos jump 3% while IT sheds 1.4%.
Sony beats a £2bn UK class action over PlayStation Store pricing; Brussels charges Temu under the DSA.

read.title: The Ledger's Read
paragraphs: Wednesday told two stories at once. On the surface the S&P 500 barely moved, but underneath it a gap of about 1.5 percentage points opened between a falling Dow and a rising Nasdaq. Old-economy and defensive pockets, health insurers, energy and miners, took the hits, while anything tied to the Anthropic deal rallied. Today the market gets its cleanest test yet of whether November's AI selloff was a reset or the start of something deeper: a $1.5 trillion company opening for trade.

Rates remain the tide underneath. The Fed's minutes and Governor Waller's talk of a half-point move push the debate from whether the Fed hikes in December to how much. The dollar's climb to a 19-month high is the clearest transmission channel: it is crushing gold, silver and copper, pressing the euro below 1.10 and the yen toward 160, and squeezing bitcoin. Today's jobless claims and Philadelphia Fed survey at 14:30 CET feed straight into that pricing.

Geopolitics is the wild card for commodities. Oil fell to its lowest WTI settle since August on a US inventory build, yet a tanker strike in Hormuz and reports that Washington is weighing a wider Iran campaign lifted Brent back above $92 overnight. The Shenzhen trilateral could cut either way for oil, chip-export rules and Hong Kong tech. For portfolios the open questions are whether the AI bid broadens beyond one IPO and whether a stronger dollar keeps draining the metals trade.

sections.name: Markets & Money
sections.intro: The finance pages: every story here ends with what it means for prices.

stories.headline: A Split Tape: Dow Drops 561 Points as the Nasdaq Edges Up
stories.summary: The S&P 500 slipped 0.23% to 7,323.63 on Wednesday, its fifth straight decline and longest losing run since June, and closed below its 200-day moving average. The Dow fell 561.25 points, or 1.11%, to 50,198.17, with UnitedHealth the biggest drag, while the Nasdaq Composite rose 0.42% to 24,429.89. Consumer discretionary was the best sector, up 1.8%, and energy the worst, down 3.3%, followed by health care at minus 2.2%. Small caps outperformed, with the Russell 2000 up 0.46%. The VIX eased to 24.56.
stories.market: Money rotated toward AI-linked and consumer names and away from insurers, energy and materials. Losing the 200-day average is a technical warning for the broad index even as tech stabilises.

stories.headline: Health Insurers Crash on a Medicare Advantage Audit Proposal
stories.summary: Managed-care stocks suffered one of their worst days in months after the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services proposed a rule that would widen audits of Medicare Advantage plans and claw back improper payments going back to 2018. Humana fell nearly 13%, UnitedHealth about 10.2%, Elevance 7.6%, Centene 7% and CVS 5.2%. Public comments on the proposal are open until 19 January 2027.
stories.market: The health-care sector lost 2.2% and was the main reason the Dow underperformed. Clawbacks would hit insurers' earnings directly, so the stocks may stay under pressure until the final rule's scope is clear.

stories.headline: TJX and Target Lift Retail; Walmart Reports Before the Bell
stories.summary: TJX jumped 8% after quarterly revenue of $15.95 billion topped estimates of $15.82 billion and it lifted its full-year earnings outlook to $5.17 to $5.20 a share. Target rose 4% after posting its strongest sales growth in five years and guiding full-year earnings to $10.65 to $11.40 a share. Lowe's added 1%. Walmart reports at 13:00 CET today, with Alibaba also before the US open.
stories.market: Off-price and big-box retailers are winning share from a value-seeking consumer. Walmart's guidance will set the tone for holiday-season expectations and consumer discretionary stocks.

stories.headline: Palo Alto Beats and Buys Applied Compute for $4.5 Billion
stories.summary: Palo Alto Networks reported fiscal first-quarter adjusted earnings of $1.05 a share, ahead of the $0.97 consensus, and agreed to acquire Applied Compute in an all-stock deal worth $4.5 billion. The shares rose 9.9% in the regular session and about 8% more after hours. The wider cybersecurity group rallied after the US cyber agency CISA urged organisations to patch a newly disclosed flaw dubbed Java4Shell: SentinelOne gained 10.4% and CrowdStrike 8%.
stories.market: Security software is the rare corner of software being bid up this month. A widely exploited flaw tends to pull forward spending on detection and response tools.

stories.headline: Europe Falls for a Third Day as Miners Slump
stories.summary: European shares extended their losing streak on Wednesday. The STOXX Europe 600 fell 1.03% to 644.05, Frankfurt's DAX lost 1.19% to 25,736.24 with SAP and Deutsche Bank among the decliners, and London's FTSE 100 dropped 1.30% to 10,551.17 as mining stocks fell between about 4.7% and 8% with copper and silver. Confirmation that euro-area inflation reached 4.0% in October added to rate worries.
stories.market: Commodity-heavy London is the most exposed to the metals rout, while the DAX now sits well below the 27,000 mark it crossed last week. Firmer US futures this morning point to a steadier open, but miners remain hostage to the dollar.

stories.headline: Indian Stocks Steady as Autos Jump and IT Slides
stories.summary: After Wednesday's 0.6% fall, when the Sensex closed at 82,031.81 and the Nifty at 25,227.95 with Titan down 5.3%, Indian benchmarks opened slightly lower on Thursday and then recovered. By 11:00 in Mumbai the Sensex was up 210 points at 82,241.80 and the Nifty up 0.25% at 25,291.65. The Nifty Auto index led with a gain of about 3%, PSU banks were firm, and Nifty IT was the weakest sector, down 1.4%, with Infosys, Tech Mahindra and HCLTech the main losers. Paytm and Pine Labs fell up to 7% on a report about fees for merchant UPI payments.
stories.market: IT stocks are reacting to the overnight weakness in US software and a stronger dollar outlook, while autos and lenders lead domestically. India VIX rose 5.6% to 16.5, a sign traders are buying protection.

stories.headline: Taiwan Plunges 4.4% While Seoul and Tokyo Hold Up
stories.summary: Asia split sharply on Thursday. Taiwan's Taiex fell 4.4% to 38,426.89, one of its largest points drops on record, as TSMC lost 3.5% and memory makers sank more than 9%; regulators cut limits on short selling and the government said its NT$500 billion stabilisation fund is ready. Hong Kong's Hang Seng was down about 1.8% at 22,871.93 in the morning and Shanghai about 0.4%. Korea's Kospi recovered from early losses to close up 1.39% at 5,137.89, helped by a Korea-China services deal and a 3.4% gain in SK hynix, while Japan's Nikkei 225 rose about 0.5% to near 59,300. In Australia, unemployment rose to 4.9%, the highest since late 2021.
stories.market: Taiwan is absorbing the brunt of the AI-chip selloff and new US export licence rules, with foreigners selling heavily and the Taiwan dollar at a 19-month low near 32.95. The Australian dollar fell about 0.6% after the jobs data.

stories.headline: Fed Minutes Point to More Hikes; Waller Raises the Half-Point Option
stories.summary: Minutes of the Fed's 27-28 October meeting, released on Wednesday, showed almost all officials judged that further rate increases would likely be appropriate, and policymakers flagged AI-related demand as an inflation risk. Governor Christopher Waller said a half-point hike in December should be considered. Prediction market Kalshi put the chance of a quarter-point move on 9 December at 91% and of a bigger one at 8%. Treasury yields still eased: the 10-year finished near 5.07%, the 2-year at 4.80% and the 30-year at 5.41%. The dollar index rose 0.29% to 103.80, a 19-month high.
stories.market: The debate has moved from whether the Fed hikes to by how much, and a 50-basis-point move is not priced. A stronger dollar is the main channel: it pressures gold, emerging-market currencies and US multinationals' earnings.

stories.headline: Ueda Signals More BoJ Hikes as the Yen Nears 160
stories.summary: Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda said the central bank expects to keep raising interest rates. In a Reuters poll, 86% of economists expect the BoJ to lift its policy rate to 1.50% at its 17-18 December meeting. The 10-year JGB yield eased about 4 basis points to around 2.83%, and the yen traded near 159.6 per dollar. October national inflation data are due at 00:30 CET on Friday.
stories.market: A December BoJ hike would narrow the rate gap with the US and could cap the dollar near 160 yen, the level where markets also watch for intervention. Japanese banks benefit from higher rates; exporters lose some of the weak-yen tailwind.

stories.headline: Euro-Area Inflation Confirmed at 4.0%, Twice the ECB Target
stories.summary: Eurostat confirmed on Wednesday that annual inflation in the euro area rose to 4.0% in October, the highest since September 2023 and double the ECB's 2% goal, with energy costs the main driver. Economists at ING said the figure brings the ECB closer to raising rates in December, and several governing council members have already backed a move.
stories.market: A December ECB hike would support the euro, which has slipped to about 1.0965 against a strong dollar, and push Bund yields higher. Rate-sensitive sectors such as real estate and utilities are most exposed.

stories.headline: Metals Rout: Gold Falls 3.5% to Its Lowest Since September 2025
stories.summary: Gold futures settled at $3,728.80 an ounce on Wednesday, down 3.5%, their lowest close since September 2025, after briefly trading below $3,700. Silver dropped 4.8% to about $45 and copper 5.2% to $5.66 a pound. The selling followed the hawkish Fed minutes and the dollar's climb to a 19-month high. Gold was about 0.4% lower again in Asian trade on Thursday, near $3,730.
stories.market: Rising real yields and a firm dollar are erasing the haven and debasement trades that drove gold to a record above $5,600 in January. Miners in London and Toronto take the hit, along with silver-heavy names.

stories.headline: WTI Hits a Three-Month Low, Then the Gulf Pushes Back
stories.summary: US crude settled down 3.2% at $83.26 a barrel on Wednesday, its lowest close since 26 August, after US inventories rose by 3.38 million barrels; Brent settled 1.3% lower at $91.95. Overnight, a loaded tanker was struck by an unidentified projectile in the Strait of Hormuz and reports said Washington was weighing wider strikes on Iran, sending Brent briefly above $93 before it settled near $92. US natural gas jumped 6.1%.
stories.market: Supply data argue for lower prices, Hormuz risk for higher ones. Energy was the S&P 500's worst sector on Wednesday; oil importers such as India gain from every dollar lower.

stories.headline: Bitcoin Slips Toward $62,000 as the Dollar Climbs
stories.summary: Bitcoin fell about 4% on Wednesday to roughly $62,300, and ether lost 3.3% to about $1,763. The largest cryptocurrency recovered slightly to around $63,700 in Asian hours on Thursday, still down about 1% on the day. The euro eased to about 1.0965 per dollar and the yen to around 159.6.
stories.market: Crypto keeps trading like a leveraged bet on easier money, and the Fed is moving the other way. A strong ANT debut could briefly help risk appetite, but rates remain the dominant driver.

stories.headline: Trump, Xi and Putin Meet in the First Three-Way Leaders' Summit
stories.summary: The leaders of the United States, China and Russia gathered in Shenzhen on Thursday, on the sidelines of the APEC summit, for what is billed as the first trilateral meeting of its kind. The agenda is expected to cover the US-Israeli war with Iran, Russia's war in Ukraine, nuclear arms control, trade and artificial intelligence. Trump told Putin the two had enjoyed a great relationship for many years as leaders posed for the APEC family photo. Officials on several sides have played down expectations of a breakthrough.
stories.market: Any easing on chip-export curbs or tariffs would help Hong Kong tech and chip-equipment makers; a joint line on Iran could take some risk premium out of oil. A visible rift would do the opposite.

stories.headline: Washington Weighs Wider Iran Strikes as Gulf Attacks Mount
stories.summary: The New York Times reported that President Trump is considering a new and extensive round of strikes on Iran, with Israel pressing for an air campaign of four to seven days; no decision has been made. Iran had targeted a US air base in Kuwait and sites in Bahrain after this week's US strike on Qeshm Island, and both countries said they intercepted the attacks. Early on Thursday a loaded tanker was hit by an unidentified projectile in the Strait of Hormuz, and debris from a Houthi missile aimed at Riyadh caused damage in the Saudi capital.
stories.market: Tanker and insurance costs stay high and Brent bounced back above $92. A broader campaign is the main upside risk for oil and a support for defence stocks and the dollar.

stories.headline: Germany's Record 2027 Budget Heads for a Final Vote
stories.summary: The Bundestag's budget committee has signed off a federal budget for 2027 of €560.9 billion, the largest in German history, after a session of more than 15 hours. Including special funds, net new borrowing exceeds €210 billion, with defence and investment receiving substantially more money while the transport budget faces cuts. The final vote in parliament is planned for the session week of 24 to 27 November. The electricity-tax cut that the coalition agreed this week is funded only for 2027.
stories.market: Heavy borrowing means more Bund supply and upward pressure on German yields, at the same time as the ECB leans toward a hike. Defence and infrastructure contractors are the clearest beneficiaries of the spending mix.

stories.headline: SAP and Deutsche Bank Weigh on Frankfurt
stories.summary: SAP and Deutsche Bank were among the heaviest decliners as the DAX fell 1.19% to 25,736.24 on Wednesday, its third losing session. Deutsche Bank is still digesting this week's reporting based on a leak of 15 million internal files, while SAP has been caught in the global selloff in software stocks.
stories.market: The DAX's two largest themes, software and banks, are both under pressure. A strong ANT debut and firmer US tech could offer SAP some relief at today's open.

stories.headline: UPI Merchant Fee Report Hits Paytm and Pine Labs
stories.summary: Shares of payments companies Paytm and Pine Labs fell as much as 7% on Thursday morning after a report about charges on merchant payments made through UPI, India's instant-payments network, which has operated largely without merchant fees. The move came as the broader market steadied, with the Nifty up about 0.25% by late morning.
stories.market: Any fee on UPI merchant transactions would change the economics of Indian fintech; the initial reaction suggests investors fear a cost or competitive hit rather than new revenue. Watch for clarification from the government or the payments regulator.

stories.headline: Mahanadi Coalfields IPO Gets a Slow Start
stories.summary: The initial public offering of Mahanadi Coalfields, a Coal India subsidiary, was subscribed only about 0.1 times by mid-morning on its first day. Institutional buyers had not yet bid, and the non-institutional and retail portions were barely touched.
stories.market: Slow first-day demand is common for large public-sector issues, which often fill late. A weak final book would weigh on sentiment toward the government's disinvestment pipeline and on Coal India shares.

stories.headline: Beijing Sets a Much Weaker Yuan Fix Than Expected
stories.summary: The People's Bank of China set its daily dollar-yuan reference rate at 6.7128 on Thursday, far weaker for the yuan than the 6.6684 that a Reuters survey had expected. The gap is unusually wide and came on the morning of the Shenzhen leaders' meeting, as the dollar trades near a 19-month high.
stories.market: A softer fix signals Beijing is willing to let the yuan weaken with the dollar's rise, which helps Chinese exporters but can unsettle regional currencies and Hong Kong-listed stocks, already down about 1.8% this morning.

stories.headline: Australian Unemployment Jumps to a Four-Year High
stories.summary: Australia's jobless rate rose to 4.9% in October from 4.7%, the highest since late 2021. Employment fell by 43,500, against forecasts for a gain of about 25,000.
stories.market: The data weaken the case for further tightening by the Reserve Bank of Australia. The Australian dollar fell about 0.6% to near 0.668 US dollars.

stories.headline: Who Wins From Anthropic's Listing
stories.summary: Anthropic's $83-a-share pricing lifted the companies closest to it on Wednesday. Amazon, which owns nearly 15%, rose 3.8%; AMD gained 5.3% and Broadcom 3.6%. Seven chip and cloud partners, including Nvidia, Microsoft, Google and Micron, are buying $26 billion of non-voting stock alongside the IPO, and existing backers such as Sequoia, Iconiq, Lightspeed, Accel and Altimeter were reported to be buying more. Rival OpenAI was last valued privately at about $1.25 trillion and has not announced listing plans.
stories.market: Public pricing of an AI model developer gives investors a new benchmark for the sector and marks up big holders such as Amazon and Alphabet. It may also intensify pressure on other private AI firms to list.

stories.headline: Nvidia Gives Back Its Gains; Moody's Trims Its Outlook
stories.summary: Nvidia fell 2.9% to about $151 on Wednesday, erasing the bounce from its better-than-expected results, after board chair Harvey Jones reiterated that Jensen Huang will not return as chief executive. Moody's changed its outlook on the company to stable, citing Huang's departure.
stories.market: Strong numbers are not enough to offset leadership uncertainty for now. Nvidia's weakness while other AI names rallied shows money spreading across the AI supply chain rather than concentrating in one stock.

sections.name: Courts & Regulators
sections.intro: Lawsuits, rulings, antitrust and enforcement that can move a company's value.

stories.headline: Sony defeats £2bn UK class action over PlayStation Store pricing
stories.summary: London's Competition Appeal Tribunal on Tuesday 17 November threw out in full a claim of nearly £2 billion (about $2.6 billion) brought by consumer advocate Alex Neill on behalf of UK PlayStation users. The claim argued that Sony abused a dominant position by forcing digital games and add-ons to be sold only through its own PlayStation Store, which allegedly kept digital prices above those of physical copies. The tribunal found the claimants had not shown a breach of competition law, rejected their market definition and held that Sony's typical commission of around 30% on digital sales was not proven to be excessive, pointing to competition from Xbox, Nintendo, PC and physical games. Sony had argued that it invested heavily in an integrated platform and that rivals use similar models. The trial began in March; Sony still faces comparable cases in the Netherlands, Portugal and Mexico.
stories.market: The ruling removes a multibillion-pound contingent liability for Sony and is a setback for UK collective actions targeting app-store and console-store commissions, a theme that also hangs over Apple, which lost a separate CAT case in October 2025 and is appealing.

sources.name: Reuters via Global Banking & Finance Review

stories.headline: Yes Bank and RBI ask India's Supreme Court to revisit ₹8,415 crore AT-1 bond ruling
stories.summary: Both Yes Bank and the Reserve Bank of India have now filed review petitions against the Supreme Court's October ruling that the March 2020 write-off of ₹8,415 crore of additional tier-1 bonds during the bank's rescue was unlawful and that the bonds must be reinstated. Yes Bank filed its review under Article 137 on 13 November, and the RBI followed with its own plea on 16 November. The RBI argues that restoring the bonds could undermine India's bank-resolution framework, clash with Basel III loss-absorption rules and dilute capital put in by SBI and other rescue investors; it also disputes the court's description of its role as that of a mere bystander. The petitions have delayed implementation, and the Supreme Court must now decide whether to admit them; bondholders are waiting for clarity on restoration.
stories.market: Yes Bank shares edged up about 1% in the session reported on 19 November as the review route keeps the reinstatement hit to profit and capital on hold; the outcome matters for India's AT-1 market and for SBI as the largest rescue investor.

stories.headline: Judge sends JPMorgan sexual-harassment suit toward a jury
stories.summary: US District Judge Lewis Kaplan in Manhattan on Wednesday 18 November refused JPMorgan Chase's request to dismiss a lawsuit by former investment banker Chirayu Rana, who alleges that executive Lorna Hajdini sexually harassed and coerced him and that the bank tolerated sexual coercion and racist abuse. JPMorgan had sought dismissal on the grounds that Rana persuaded his sister and a friend to give false witness accounts; the sister later recanted. Kaplan said whether her original account or her recantation is true is a matter for a jury, and criticised both sides for treating the case partly as a public-relations battle. JPMorgan and Hajdini deny the claims, and Hajdini has countersued Rana for defamation.
stories.market: Financially immaterial for JPMorgan, but a trial would keep governance and workplace-conduct headlines alive for the largest US bank at a time when investors weigh conduct risk alongside its earnings strength.

stories.headline: Character.AI's bankruptcy sale gets a privacy watchdog before user chats can change hands
stories.summary: Judge Brendan Shannon of the US Bankruptcy Court in Delaware on 17 November ordered the appointment of a consumer privacy ombudsman in the Chapter 11 sale of chatbot maker Character.AI, after objections from the US Trustee and a coalition of 39 states plus Washington, D.C. Disney Worldwide Services is the $20 million stalking-horse bidder for a licence to Character.AI's intellectual property, while Smirks and Pangs Acquisition LLC has bid $10 million for the app, models and user data. The bid deadline is 24 November, with an auction on 1 December and a sale hearing set for 3-4 December; the ombudsman's report is due about a week before that hearing.
stories.market: The case is an early test of how US courts treat user conversation data as a sellable asset when an AI start-up fails, with implications for valuations of consumer-AI companies; for Disney the bid is small but signals interest in AI character IP.

stories.headline: Brussels accuses Temu of failing to stop illegal products, raising risk of a second DSA fine
stories.summary: The European Commission on 17 November issued preliminary findings that Temu breached Article 35 of the Digital Services Act by not taking effective steps against the sale of illegal products. It cited three weaknesses: product compliance checks that cover only a very small share of items and rarely prioritise high-risk categories such as toys, electronics and cosmetics; content moderation focused on listings rather than safety; and sanctions aimed at individual storefronts rather than the traders behind them. Commission mystery shopping found many chargers failing basic electrical safety tests and baby toys posing medium-to-high risks. If confirmed, the breach could bring a fine of up to 6% of global annual turnover; Temu was already fined €200 million under the DSA in May 2026 for weak risk assessment. Temu can now reply in writing; no decision date has been set.
stories.market: A second penalty would add to regulatory pressure on Temu owner PDD Holdings in Europe and keep scrutiny high on low-cost cross-border marketplaces generally.

stories.headline: SEBI weighs stock-level caps on margin trading as leveraged book hits ₹1.53 lakh crore
stories.summary: SEBI chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey said on 18 November, at the World Federation of Exchanges meeting in Mumbai, that the regulator is still considering proposals to tighten the margin trading facility and has not yet decided. One option is to stop brokers funding fresh purchases in a stock once margin-funded holdings exceed a threshold of public float, reportedly between 5% and 10%; investors could still buy with their own money. Outstanding MTF positions stand at about ₹1.53 lakh crore, up 29% in a year, with more than 220 stocks above 5% of free float and 36 above 10%; small and mid caps account for nearly two-thirds of the book. SEBI is expected to consult publicly before any rule. Pandey also said extended trading hours are not feasible in India given cyber risks.
stories.market: Caps would hit the most leveraged small- and mid-cap names hardest and could curb a fast-growing revenue line for brokers that fund client positions; the concern is forced selling when brokers call in loans.

stories.headline: Germany's cartel office fines landfill-liner suppliers €5.5m for 16-year quota cartel
stories.summary: The Bundeskartellamt has fined three suppliers of geosynthetic liners used to seal German landfill sites a total of about €5.5 million: G quadrat (Krefeld), Naue Sealing (Espelkamp) and KAT Kunststoff-Abdichtungs-Systeme (Wiesmoor). From 2007 at the latest, Naue, G quadrat and Solmax Geosynthetics split landfill projects by fixed quotas of roughly 35%, 25% and 40%, used cover bids and agreed target and minimum prices, until a dawn raid broke up one of their meetings at a conference hotel on 12 September 2023. Solmax escaped a fine as leniency applicant; the other three settled and the decisions are final. The office says the four firms are the only BAM-approved suppliers of such liners in Germany, and president Andreas Mundt warned that such cartels can inflate prices for public contracting authorities.
stories.market: The firms are private, so there is no listed-stock impact, but municipalities and waste operators that awarded landfill-sealing contracts since 2007 may now pursue damages claims.

stories.headline: Family Dollar's $63m pricing settlement widens as Dollar General fight continues
stories.summary: The Federal Trade Commission and 17 states have reached a proposed $63 million settlement with Family Dollar over charges that its stores rang up higher prices at checkout than on shelves, tags, its website or app. The package includes a $40 million consumer redress fund, a $20 million customer discount programme and more than $3 million for the states, plus an independently certified pricing-accuracy programme. Alabama's attorney general publicised the state's participation on 16 November. Family Dollar neither admitted nor denied the allegations. A separate FTC and multistate lawsuit filed in October against Dollar General over similar overcharging claims remains pending.
stories.market: The settlement sets a benchmark for what the still-litigating Dollar General could face and adds to compliance costs across discount retail.

sections.name: Shadow Markets
sections.intro: Grey-market premiums, parallel currencies, illicit trade, fraud and private credit.

stories.headline: Grey market cools on Coal India's Mahanadi unit as Crystal Crop holds a premium
stories.summary: Unofficial grey-market premiums point to a muted debut for Mahanadi Coalfields, whose Rs 8,981 crore issue is an offer for sale by Coal India priced at Rs 129-136 a share and runs to 23 November, with listing pencilled in for 27 November. Trackers showed the GMP sliding from about Rs 9.25 on 14 November to Rs 3.10 (about 2.3%) on 18 November, and to roughly Rs 2.50 early on 19 November, implying an indicative debut near Rs 138-139. Agrochemicals maker Crystal Crop Protection, whose Rs 455 crore issue (Rs 259-272 band) closes on 20 November, fares better: its GMP stood near Rs 17-18, or roughly 6-7% over the top of the band. Crystal Crop's book was 1.48 times covered by mid-morning on 19 November, led by institutions at 2.07 times, ahead of a planned 26 November listing. GMP is an unregulated, indicative gauge and has often diverged from actual listing prices.
stories.market: A low single-digit premium on the year's largest PSU sale sets a soft tone for Coal India (COALINDIA) as the selling parent and for upcoming mainboard issues; Crystal Crop's listing will be read against agrochemical peers.

stories.headline: Argentina's financial dollar breaks ARS 1,700, gap to official rate hits 2026 high
stories.summary: The 'contado con liquidación' (CCL) dollar, the rate used to move money abroad through securities, traded around ARS 1,716 on Wednesday 18 November, roughly 8.6% above the Banco Nación retail rate of ARS 1,580 and more than 10% above the wholesale rate of ARS 1,559 - the widest gap of the year. The MEP rate was near ARS 1,621 and the informal 'blue' dollar was quoted around ARS 1,630, a record in nominal terms according to El Cronista. Local analysts cited doubts over the central bank's ability to build reserves, January debt payments, a weaker Brazilian real near 5.80 per dollar and a firmer global dollar. The BCRA bought US$74 million on Tuesday and US$277 million so far in November, with gross reserves at about US$49.7 billion.
stories.market: A widening CCL spread is a stress signal for the peso (ARS) and for Argentine sovereign dollar bonds and ADRs, which are priced off the financial exchange rate.

stories.headline: Naira slides to weakest street rate since January; Iran's open-market rial near 2.7 million
stories.summary: Lagos bureau-de-change dealers sold dollars at N1,470 on 19 November, the naira's weakest parallel-market level since 28 January and N40 weaker than on 13 November. The official NFEM rate closed Wednesday at N1,363.23, leaving a gap of about N107. Nigeria's reserves were US$43.64 billion on 14 November, down about 4% this year, and the central bank and NNPC signed an MoU on Wednesday aimed at boosting oil-related FX inflows. In Tehran, the free-market dollar sold for about 2.71 million rials on 19 November, up 1.5% on the day, versus the central bank's official rate of about 1.94 million - an open-market premium of roughly 40%.
stories.market: Widening black-market spreads signal FX scarcity for NGN and IRR; for Nigeria they matter for Eurobond and local-debt investors weighing convertibility risk.

stories.headline: EU blacklists 113 more shadow-fleet operators as false-flagged tanker heads for the Baltic
stories.summary: The EU added 12 individuals and 101 entities to its Russia sanctions list on 16 November, targeting shipowners, managers, traders and insurers in the UAE, Oman, Seychelles and China that it says move Russian oil, alongside nearly 50 Russian banks and financial firms. Those hit include Dubai-based Lidoil and Spikoil, several Dubai ship managers, Moscow insurer Balance Insurance and the operator of the Petersburg Oil Terminal. Separately, the EU's naval mission IRINI boarded the tanker MIDAG in the Mediterranean on 13 November and found it was flying a false Zimbabwean flag, but did not detain it. The empty ship was heading for the Skagen strait, with arrival expected around 23 November, prompting Kyiv's sanctions envoy to call for detentions and personal liability for captains.
stories.market: Each round of shadow-fleet listings raises freight and insurance costs on Russian crude and widens the Urals discount to Brent; tanker owners and Gulf trading hubs face rising compliance risk.

stories.headline: Pressure builds for DOJ probe into what Nvidia knew about AI-chip smuggling
stories.summary: A coalition of former national-security officials and AI policy figures wrote to Attorney General Todd Blanche on 18 November urging an investigation into Nvidia's knowledge of, and response to, smuggling of its controlled chips to China. The same day, House Foreign Affairs chairman Brian Mast asked Commerce export-control chief Jeff Kessler for end-use check results in Asia and all licences tied to Singapore-linked Megaspeed and Speedmatrix, with answers due by 1 December. Media reports allege Nvidia's general counsel contacted Kessler about the Megaspeed inquiry; a joint Commerce-DOJ statement on 16 November said Commerce had sought Megaspeed sales records from Nvidia in May 2025. Former CEO Jensen Huang is due before the committee on 1 December and general counsel Tim Teter on 2 December.
stories.market: Legal and export-control overhang for Nvidia (NVDA) and server makers such as Super Micro (SMCI), which has been indicted in a related matter; tighter enforcement could also hit Asian server-distribution channels.

stories.headline: OFAC hits Hezbollah-linked gold traders in Lebanon and Istanbul
stories.summary: The US Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control added three individuals and three entities to its terrorism sanctions list on 18 November, all tied to Hezbollah. They include two precious-metals businesses - Lebanon-based Gold Global Company and Istanbul jeweller Sankari Gold Kuyumculuk - both linked to designated individual Hassan Khechen, plus a Lebanese association. The action falls under Treasury's 'Operation Economic Outcast' campaign against Iran's proxy and financing networks. US persons are barred from dealing with the listed parties and any of their assets under US jurisdiction are frozen.
stories.market: The listings add to compliance scrutiny of the cash-heavy gold trade linking Lebanon, Turkey and the Gulf, a channel regulators see as a route for moving sanctioned money.

stories.headline: Founders of Indiana forex fund charged over alleged $600 million Ponzi scheme
stories.summary: Manhattan federal prosecutors on 18 November unsealed charges against Phillip Patrick Williams, 51, and Devin Allen Johnson, 29, founders of Backward Hat Capital, over an alleged Ponzi-like scheme. The firm, set up around 2022, marketed funds that it said traded currencies with a proprietary algorithm and typically promised more than 6% a month, raising over $600 million from more than 2,000 investors. Prosecutors allege the trading was largely illusory, that more than $200 million of new money paid earlier investors' redemptions, and that over $130 million went to Williams and over $40 million to Johnson. Both were arrested, and the SEC and CFTC filed parallel civil cases; the charges are allegations only.
stories.market: Another blow to retail-marketed FX and algorithmic-trading products; cases like this tend to tighten scrutiny of unregistered fund offerings and the audits behind them.

stories.headline: DeFi vaults drained of $3.9 million as Binance hacker wallet stirs again
stories.summary: Security firm Blockaid flagged two exploits on 18 November that cost about $3.88 million combined. Attackers used wstETH flash loans to manipulate liquidations in K3 Capital's sBOLD vault on Ethereum, a third-party product built on Liquity V2, taking about $3.43 million. On Polygon, real-estate tokenisation platform Reental lost about $454,000 after an administrator upgraded deposit-token contracts to code that let anyone withdraw the stablecoins. Separately, the address behind the October Binance hot-wallet exploit moved 34,279.66 ETH to three fresh wallets on 17 November after about two weeks of inactivity, according to on-chain tracker MistTrack.
stories.market: Movement of large stolen ETH balances is watched as potential selling pressure on Ether (ETH) and for laundering through mixers and bridges; repeated vault exploits weigh on DeFi lending tokens.

stories.headline: BoE widens private-credit stress test as HPS chases $9.5 billion for new direct-lending fund
stories.kicker: Private credit · UK, US, euro area
stories.summary: The Bank of England is extending its system-wide exploratory scenario on private markets to model how a severe downturn could spread through banks, insurers and funds, including whether lenders would cut credit lines once funds gate redemptions; more than 40 firms, among them Apollo, Ares, Blackstone and KKR, were surveyed, with a final report due in the first half of 2027. The ECB's Financial Stability Review on 18 November likewise flagged liquidity and leverage weaknesses in some non-banks and tighter bank-non-bank links as shock amplifiers. Redemption pressure persists: investors pulled about $12.7 billion from non-traded BDCs in the first half, and Blackstone's BCRED saw requests of about 10% of shares in the June quarter, double its usual 5% cap. Fundraising continues regardless, with BlackRock's HPS seeking $9.5 billion of equity for Specialty Loan Fund VII and targeting a first close in early 2027.
stories.market: Supervisory focus and gated redemptions weigh on alternative managers (BX, APO, ARES, KKR, OWL) and listed BDCs, while fresh institutional fundraising supports BlackRock (BLK).

sections.name: Deals, Earnings & Street Calls
sections.intro: M&A and capital markets, the results scorecard, and what analysts and big money are doing.

stories.headline: ICEYE's €2bn cash bid for Avio runs into a cool reception in Rome
stories.summary: Finnish satellite operator ICEYE has launched an all-cash tender offer for Italian rocket maker Avio at €41 per share. The offer values Avio at about €2.05 billion and is 21.3% above its 16 November close. Defence Minister Guido Crosetto told Reuters that state-controlled Leonardo, which owns about 18% of Avio, should think hard before selling. Officials said Rome had not yet been formally notified and would run the full national-interest review under its 'golden power' rules. Leonardo CEO Lorenzo Mariani called himself pleasantly surprised by the bid, and broker Equita sees a good chance of approval, possibly with Leonardo keeping a stake. ICEYE's CEO expects the deal to take several more months to close.
stories.market: Avio rose about 1.5% to €39.75 on Wednesday. It still trades roughly 3% below the €41 offer, a gap that reflects political and approval risk. The outcome is a test for cross-border consolidation in Europe's defence and space sector.

stories.headline: BASF tries a jobs-and-sites pact to revive its Evonik pursuit
stories.summary: Handelsblatt has reported a BASF draft dated 11 November, titled 'Zukunftspakt'. In it, BASF offers to keep Evonik's employee agreements in place, run the Marl and Wesseling chemical parks, and keep Essen as a major site, home to a board division responsible for more than €10 billion in revenue. Insiders say many of the commitments go little beyond what already exists. Evonik has already rejected BASF's indicated €24 per share, which values it at more than €11 billion, and says it is not in talks. Market chatter puts a level that might restart talks at €26-28, but BASF has not tabled a higher bid. North Rhine-Westphalia premier Hendrik Wüst came out against a takeover, citing Evonik's roughly 11,000 jobs in the state.
stories.market: Evonik traded around €21.92 late Wednesday, slightly lower, and is up about 64% this year on bid hopes. LBBW raised its target to €23 from €22 and kept a Hold rating.

stories.headline: Fairfax sells IIFL Finance stake in ₹3,413-crore block to fund its IDBI Bank purchase
stories.summary: About 5.61 crore IIFL Finance shares, roughly 13.15% of the company, changed hands in Wednesday's pre-open session in a block worth about ₹3,413 crore. The floor price was ₹611, a 3.9% discount to Tuesday's close. The seller was FIH Mauritius, Fairfax Financial's investment arm, which is exiting its whole 13.25% holding. Business Standard reports the proceeds will help pay for Fairfax's proposed purchase of 60.72% of IDBI Bank from the government and LIC for ₹52,878 crore. FIH also completed its open offer for IIFL Capital Services on 18 November and becomes promoter there from 19 November, with 38.04%. It plans to buy 3 million more shares from promoter-group entities.
stories.market: IIFL Finance shares rose about 6% to ₹676 in early trade as the overhang cleared. IDBI Bank and IIFL Capital stay in focus as the Fairfax transactions move ahead.

stories.headline: US capital raises punished: Hyster-Yale converts, CVR notes, Applied Opto share-sale programme
stories.summary: Hyster-Yale proposed $125 million of convertible notes due 2031, with an option for $18.75 million more. Most of the money will repay $100 million of a $213.2 million term loan, and up to $15 million goes to buybacks and capped calls. CVR Energy plans $1.25 billion of senior secured notes due 2032 to help fund refinery acquisitions in Minnesota and North Dakota. Applied Optoelectronics set up an at-the-market programme to sell up to $550 million of stock, about 15% of its market value. In Ardent Health, holders Equity Group Investments and Ventas priced 8 million shares at $14.50, and the company is buying back 1.5 million of them. On the buyback side, Amer Sports authorised $1 billion, Bullish $300 million and Hesai $100 million.
stories.market: Hyster-Yale closed down about 41%, Ardent about 19% and Applied Optoelectronics about 10%. CVR fell about 11% intraday. Bullish and Hesai gained about 6% and 3% on their buybacks.

stories.headline: US antitrust enforcers open the door to behavioural merger fixes
stories.summary: Charlie Beller, a deputy assistant attorney general in the Justice Department's antitrust division, told a New York conference that DOJ will now treat company pledges about future conduct as a factor that can ease competition concerns. Asset sales are no longer the only remedy it will accept, especially where divestitures are hard to arrange. The shift follows DOJ's 6 November decision to close its review of Fox's $22 billion Roku deal on the strength of carriage and data commitments. Those commitments were never filed in court. Bloomberg notes the stance could shape DOJ's review of Nvidia's $13 billion purchase of Hugging Face. At the same event, the FTC's David Shaw said behavioural remedies remain disfavoured and rare there, though he accepted that blocking a deal is not always the best outcome. House Democrats want to tighten Tunney Act disclosure rules.
stories.market: A softer remedy policy at DOJ lowers the risk of a deal being blocked outright, which matters for merger-arbitrage spreads on large pending US tech and media deals. The FTC's more cautious tone means the outcome will depend on which agency reviews a deal.

stories.headline: Crystal Crop IPO covered 1.46 times on day one as India's primary pipeline fills
stories.summary: Agrochemicals maker Crystal Crop Protection opened its ₹455.49-crore IPO on 18 November. The deal is a ₹354.77-crore fresh issue plus a ₹100.71-crore offer for sale, priced at ₹259-272 a share. By the end of day one it was subscribed 1.46 times: QIBs 2.11x, retail 1.35x and non-institutional investors 0.79x. The issue closes on 20 November and is due to list on BSE and NSE on 26 November. Grey-market premium estimates ranged from ₹13 to ₹19, or about 5-7% above the top of the band. Also in this week's pipeline, the SME issue Watrana Rentals opens on 19 November and aims to raise ₹120 crore.
stories.market: A moderate premium and day-one demand led by institutions point to steady but selective appetite for Indian IPOs. Agrochemical peers may trade off the final subscription numbers.

stories.headline: Europe's results day: Hays soars, Alstom slumps, Experian and SSE deliver
stories.summary: Hays said first-half operating profit will be at least £35 million, against a consensus of £24.8 million, helped by better German net fees. Alstom swung to a first-half net loss of €954 million after charges on delayed German regional-train contracts, and its net debt rose to €1.10 billion. Alstom is now studying about €2 billion of deleveraging by September 2027, which could include disposals or equity funding. Experian lifted benchmark EPS 15% to 97.5 cents, added a $500 million buyback and guided to 6-7% organic growth. SSE's adjusted pretax profit jumped 91% to about £1.0 billion and adjusted EPS reached 66.5p, with full-year guidance of 168-193p unchanged. Convatec raised its 2026 revenue-growth range to 6.25-7.00%. British Land raised its EPS guidance to 31.0p. Workspace's loss widened and it skipped its interim dividend, while Jet2's operating profit fell 18% to £588.3 million.
stories.market: Hays rose 23% to about 68p and Convatec 9%, while Alstom fell more than 8% in Paris and Workspace 7%. Experian added about 2.4% and British Land gained about 1.8%.

stories.headline: AI hardware beats: Everpure and Kulicke & Soffa top forecasts, Dolby guides low
stories.summary: Everpure, the former Pure Storage, reported fiscal Q3 revenue of $1.46 billion against an expected $1.33 billion, up 51%, and adjusted EPS of $0.86 against $0.67. It raised its full-year revenue outlook to $5.20-5.21 billion from $5.03-5.07 billion, and its remaining performance obligations rose 44% to $4.2 billion. Chip-packaging equipment maker Kulicke & Soffa posted revenue of $410.3 million against an expected $376.4 million and non-GAAP EPS of $1.52 against $1.41. It guided next quarter to about $410 million in revenue and about $1.65 in EPS. On 17 November, Dolby beat on Q4 with adjusted EPS of $1.25 against $1.19. Its Q1 revenue guide of $285-305 million was far below the $359 million consensus, though its full-year EPS range of $4.27-4.42 was slightly above estimates.
stories.market: Everpure gained about 4% after hours, while Dolby lost about 3% after its outlook. Magnera rose 15% after hours on its FY2027 EBITDA guidance of $390-410 million, and Universal Technical Institute fell 8.6% on a cautious FY2027 margin plan.

stories.headline: Wednesday's US earnings swings: BellRing jumps, Jumia and Prenetics collapse
stories.summary: BellRing Brands, which makes protein shakes, posted Q4 net sales of $692 million against an expected $658.5 million, while adjusted EPS of 22 cents was a cent short. Its FY2027 adjusted EBITDA midpoint of $330 million was above the $317.1 million consensus. Jumia's Q3 revenue rose 33% to $60.7 million, but it cut its full-year forecast after weak early Black Friday sales. Kornit Digital grew revenue about 10% to $58.3 million and guided Q4 to $60-65 million. Prenetics widened its expected second-half adjusted EBITDA loss to $30-35 million from $8-12 million, despite revenue tripling to $64.1 million. i3 Verticals guided FY2027 revenue to $220-235 million.
stories.market: BellRing closed up 24%, though it remains well down for the year, and i3 Verticals gained 12%. Jumia fell 41%, Prenetics 42% intraday and Kornit 23%.

stories.headline: UBS cuts US stocks to neutral even as it sets an 8,200 S&P 500 target for 2027
stories.summary: In its 2027 outlook, published 18 November, UBS Global Wealth Management cut US equities to Neutral from Overweight and moved global equities to Neutral as well. It sees the S&P 500 at 8,200 by end-2027, about 12% above Wednesday's close of 7,323.63. UBS expects S&P 500 earnings growth to slow from about 29% in 2026 to around 15% in 2027. It warns about lofty profit expectations, competition and substitution risk around AI, and concentration, with the ten largest stocks making up about 40% of the index. UBS names the euro area as its top region, with a Euro Stoxx 50 target of 7,000, and favours large cloud providers and leading chip-equipment makers. Goldman Sachs' Ben Snider has a base case of 8,700 for the S&P 500.
stories.market: A major house turning neutral on the US while preferring the euro area supports the case for rotation into European equities. It also adds caution around mega-cap tech after a mixed session for the Nasdaq and the Dow.

stories.headline: Broker calls: Siemens cut by Oddo, Air France-KLM target nearly doubled, Voestalpine and Whitbread upgraded
stories.summary: Oddo BHF cut Siemens to Neutral from Outperform with a €302 target, while Citi raised its target to €340 from €335 and kept a Buy rating. Santander moved Air France-KLM from Underperform to Outperform and lifted its target to €17 from €9.30. Goldman Sachs upgraded Whitbread to Buy with a 3,700p target, but cut Technip Energies to Neutral. Jefferies upgraded Voestalpine to Buy and cut its target to €48 from €52. On 19 November Voestalpine reported H1 EBITDA of €846 million, including about €100 million of one-offs, and trimmed its full-year EBITDA range to €1.60-1.70 billion from €1.60-1.85 billion. In the US, Stifel cut Insulet to Hold, Citi cut the New York Times to Neutral, and JPMorgan slashed its Alnylam target to $254 from $369.
stories.market: Siemens slipped 1.7% to about €266, while Air France-KLM rose 2.1% to €14.84 and Whitbread 2.7%. Voestalpine gained about 1% on the upgrade before its results.

stories.headline: Foreign investors buy Indian stocks for a 13th straight session as Nifty options cluster at 25,000-26,000
stories.summary: Foreign institutional investors were net buyers of ₹5,866.78 crore of Indian cash equities on 18 November, their 13th consecutive day of buying. Domestic institutions were net sellers of ₹3,159.90 crore, leaving combined net buying of about ₹2,707 crore. The Nifty still fell 0.63% to 25,227.95. The India VIX ended at 15.57, little changed. In options for the 23 November weekly expiry, the largest call open interest sits near 26,000 and the largest put open interest near 25,000. The put-call ratio for that expiry stands at a low 0.75.
stories.market: Steady foreign inflows are cushioning Indian equities and the rupee against weak global cues. The options positioning suggests traders expect the Nifty to stay between roughly 25,000 and 26,000 in the near term.

sections.name: Around the World
sections.intro: The top story from each major economy, with its market angle.

stories.headline: UK inflation climbs to 3.6%, a one-year high, but undershoots the Bank of England
stories.summary: UK consumer prices rose 3.6% in the year to October, up from 3.5% in September and the highest reading in a year, the ONS said on Wednesday 18 November. Fuel and other transport costs did most of the pushing, while core inflation held at 2.8% and food inflation eased to 0.9% from 1.3%. CPIH rose to 3.7%. The headline print matched market estimates but came in below the Bank of England's own projection, as did services inflation. The BoE raised Bank Rate by a quarter point to 4% on 5 November and its latest Monetary Policy Report warned inflation could approach 5% around mid-2027, so a further hike in December remains under debate.
stories.market: Sterling fell as much as 0.6% to about $1.3136, its weakest since late November 2025, as traders pared bets on further tightening, and gilt yields dropped to a six-day low. MUFG still expects a December hike and called the pound's dip a short-term setback.

stories.headline: Brussels says France will overshoot its deficit goals as growth stalls
stories.summary: The European Commission's autumn forecast, published on Tuesday 17 November, puts France's 2026 budget deficit at 5.5% of GDP and 2027 at 5.4%, against Paris's own 2027 goal of 5%. With no policy change the gap widens again to 5.7% in 2028. Growth is pencilled in at only 0.4% this year and 0.6% next, the weakest in the euro zone, while public debt climbs from 115.7% of GDP in 2025 to 122.1% in 2027 and 123.2% in 2028. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu's 2027 budget relies on roughly EUR 54 billion of savings, and around 146,000 people marched over living costs the same day. For the euro area as a whole, the Commission sees 1.2% growth and a 3.5% deficit this year.
stories.market: The forecast keeps pressure on French government bonds (OATs) and their spread over German Bunds, and weighs on rate-sensitive French banks and domestically exposed stocks on the CAC 40.

stories.headline: Rome leans towards waving through Intesa's bid for Monte dei Paschi without conditions
stories.summary: Italy's government is reportedly inclined to approve Intesa Sanpaolo's exchange offer for Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena without using its 'golden power' veto rights or attaching binding conditions, Reuters reported on 18 November. Intesa offers 1.664 new Intesa shares plus EUR 1.25 in cash for each MPS share and has ruled out raising the cash part again. The MPS board under Luigi Lovaglio gives its opinion on 20 November, the acceptance window opens on 24 November and runs to 22 January 2027, and the antitrust verdict is due in early December. Remedies under study reportedly include selling about 100 of MPS's 625 branches. Santander analysts expect the 66.7% acceptance threshold to be cleared.
stories.market: MPS traded around EUR 11.21 on Thursday morning; the deal sets up Italy's largest bank to absorb its oldest and shifts focus to the stake MPS holds in Generali.

stories.headline: Brussels lifts Spain's growth outlook to 2.6%, but flags sticky inflation
stories.summary: The European Commission's autumn forecast on 17 November raised Spain's 2026 growth estimate to 2.6%, 0.2 percentage points above its spring call, making it one of the euro zone's strongest performers. It sees growth easing to 2.1% in 2027 and 1.9% in 2028, slightly below Madrid's own projections of 2.2% and 2.1%. Inflation is forecast to average 3.9% this year and 3.3% next. The deficit is expected at 2.6% of GDP in 2026, falling to 2.2% by 2028, with public debt dipping below 100% of GDP.
stories.market: Spain's relative strength supports its narrow bond spread over Bunds and domestic cyclicals on the IBEX 35, though above-target inflation keeps pressure on real incomes.

stories.headline: Cevian sells a quarter of its UBS stake as capital fight nears a vote
stories.summary: Stockholm-based activist Cevian Capital sold about 26% of its UBS holding, or 12.6 million shares, in the three months to end-September, filings showed on 17 November, leaving it with roughly 1% of the bank. The sale comes as Bern pushes tougher capital rules after the 2023 Credit Suisse collapse; one option before the lower house of parliament, which could vote in December, would require UBS to hold about $16 billion of extra equity. UBS says that would badly damage its business model, and CEO Sergio Ermotti has hinted the bank could consider moving its headquarters. A Reuters report that UBS is preparing to accept defeat in the debate also weighed on the shares.
stories.market: UBS fell 3.34% on Tuesday, leading the SMI's 1.43% drop to 14,976; the capital decision is the key swing factor for UBS's buyback capacity.

stories.headline: Equinor hit by cyberattack as krone slides to bottom of G10 table
stories.summary: Equinor, Europe's biggest gas supplier, disclosed on the evening of 17 November an ongoing cyberattack on internal IT and business software, and alerted Norway's National Security Authority and offshore regulator Havtil. The company said there was no sign of data theft and no disruption to platforms, plants or oil and gas output, and on 18 November said it better understood how the attack was carried out. Norway supplied 52.1% of the EU's pipeline gas imports in 2025, and the country raised its cyber threat level to the second-highest tier in October. Separately, ING noted the krone has been the weakest G10 currency since early November, down 4.7% against the dollar and 3.3% against the euro, as oil prices fell and Norges Bank turned more cautious on further hikes.
stories.market: Any hint of supply disruption would hit TTF gas prices; for now the bigger driver is the krone, with ING seeing EUR/NOK risks skewed towards 10.70-10.75 in the coming weeks.

stories.headline: Ukraine edges towards $1.6bn IMF tranche as 2027 funding gap looms
stories.summary: The in-person IMF mission on the second and third reviews of Ukraine's $8.1 billion Extended Fund Facility wrapped up in Warsaw, with both sides reporting good progress and talks continuing virtually, Kyiv's Finance Ministry said on 18 November. Ukraine met all end-September quantitative targets, but the $1.6 billion payout still needs financing assurances from international partners and IMF board approval; about $2.2 billion has been disbursed so far. The Fund now sees GDP shrinking 0.5% in 2026 and a further 1% in 2027, and puts the remaining financing gap at $32-34 billion for 2027 and $17 billion for 2028. It urged Kyiv to lift domestic revenue in the 2027 budget, curb the shadow economy and protect National Bank of Ukraine independence.
stories.market: The tranche hinges on Western donors closing the 2027 gap, which matters for Ukraine's restructured eurobonds and GDP warrants and for confidence in the hryvnia.

stories.headline: Putin talks up resilience at APEC while Moscow stocks slip
stories.summary: At the APEC gathering in China, Vladimir Putin on 18 November said Western sanctions had failed and claimed the economy had grown more than 10% over three years, even as his own Economic Development Ministry forecasts just 0.4% growth for 2026 after 1% in 2025. The MOEX Russia index fell 1.28% to 2,469.93 on Wednesday, giving back Tuesday's 1% gain, with miners and energy names leading losses: Nornickel dropped 3.01%, Polyus 2.76% and Gazprom 2.39%. The Bank of Russia set the official dollar rate at 82.23 rubles for 19 November, while the euro was fixed at 90.36.
stories.market: Broker forecasts cited by TASS see the ruble holding at 81-83 per dollar this week; mining and energy stocks remain the weak spots on the MOEX.

stories.headline: Senate Republicans fall short on $350bn defense reconciliation push as 11 December shutdown deadline nears
stories.summary: Senate Republicans lack the votes to bring up a budget resolution this week, all but ending hopes of passing a third party-line reconciliation package before Thanksgiving, the Washington Sun reported on 18 November. The bill would have carried roughly $350 billion for defense; Republicans can lose only three votes, and at least five senators, including Collins, Murkowski, Paul, Tillis and Cassidy, are opposed or skeptical. Majority Leader John Thune called the vote count an open question, and leaders are shifting to bipartisan talks on defense money. Federal funding runs out on 11 December, and Sen. John Kennedy put shutdown odds at roughly even or better. Republicans lost nine Senate seats in the midterms, and Democrats, who want the funding fight to pressure an end to the Iran war, take the majority in the new Congress.
stories.market: Defense contractors lose a fast-track path to a large funding top-up and now depend on regular appropriations. A December shutdown would also delay federal data releases that rate markets lean on.

stories.headline: Canadian inflation holds at 3.1%, below forecasts, splitting views on a December Bank of Canada hike
stories.summary: Canada's annual inflation rate held at 3.1% in October, Statistics Canada said on 17 November, slightly below the 3.2% economists expected and the Bank of Canada's 3.4% fourth-quarter projection. Gasoline was up 30.9% on the year, largely a base effect from a 4.8% drop in October 2025, while it fell 2.5% from September. Underlying pressure stayed mild: CPI-median held at 2.0% and CPI-trim eased to 1.8%. The central bank lifted its policy rate to 2.5% on 28 October, its first hike since July 2023, and economists are divided on another move on 9 December. Separately, the Bank announced on 16 November that Governor Tiff Macklem will step down in June 2027.
stories.market: A softer core picture weakens the case for back-to-back hikes, which matters for short-dated Canadian yields and the loonie. BMO said nothing in the data pointed clearly to a hike, while RBC called the decision finely balanced.

stories.headline: Sheinbaum says US trade talks 'very far along' after Trump meeting as peso and Mexican stocks slide
stories.summary: Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum met Donald Trump on 18 November on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen and said afterwards that bilateral trade talks were very far along. Mexico's immediate goal is relief from US Section 232 tariffs on steel, aluminium and autos; a deputy economy minister said about 80% of Mexican exports already enter the US tariff-free. Washington declined in July to extend the USMCA for a new 16-year term, and Trump last week threatened to double tariffs unless Mexico halts migrant caravans. The two countries traded about $779 billion in goods in the first nine months of the year, and Sheinbaum expects to see Trump again at the G20 in Miami in December. INEGI publishes third-quarter GDP on 23 November.
stories.market: The peso weakened about 2.3% to roughly 18.85 per dollar on Wednesday and the S&P/BMV IPC fell 1.75% to 69,154, its steepest drop since 5 June, as a stronger dollar hit metals: Peñoles lost 8.4% and Grupo México 6.3%.

stories.headline: Brazil's Senate passes spending-curb bill 69-2 as the real sinks to a six-month low
stories.summary: Brazil's Senate on 18 November gave final approval, by 69 votes to 2, to complementary bill PLP 299/2026, which caps real federal spending growth at 2% instead of 2.5% in years when containment measures are triggered. The government estimates the package improves the 2027 primary result by R$45.1-56.1 billion, though no revised figure was given after senators added changes, including doubling the annual Lei Kandir transfer floor to states to R$2 billion. The bill now goes to the Chamber of Deputies, with no vote date set. The central bank held the Selic at 13.75% on 4 November, ending a run of five cuts, and next meets on 9 December. Fiscal worries rather than global factors were blamed for the sell-off.
stories.market: The Ibovespa fell 1.34% to 167,538, nearly 20% below its 9 October peak, with Banco do Brasil down 3.4%, Vale 2.2% and Petrobras 1.8%; the dollar closed near R$5.88, its highest settlement in at least six months, while the dollar index rose only 0.44%.

stories.headline: Andean slowdown: Chile's economy shrinks 1.1% and Colombia's growth stalls at 0.5%
stories.summary: Chile's GDP fell 1.1% year on year in the third quarter, worse than the 0.8% drop expected and the biggest annual fall since late 2022, the central bank said on 18 November; it shrank 1.8% from the previous quarter, with mining the main drag and investment falling. Finance Minister Jorge Quiroz had already acknowledged a technical recession on 11 November. In Colombia, DANE said on 17 November that the economy grew just 0.5% from a year earlier, down from 3.6% in the second quarter and the weakest in two and a half years, and contracted 0.8% on the quarter. Colombian agriculture fell 6.7%, with coffee down 11.2%, while imports jumped 9.8% and exports slipped 1.8%.
stories.market: Chile's IPSA lost about 1.1% to 10,363 on Wednesday with the dollar near 1,007 pesos, while Colombia's official dollar rate was set 0.5% higher at 3,326.96 pesos for 19 November; weak copper-linked growth keeps the Chilean peso sensitive to metal prices.

stories.headline: IEA: $40bn of Gulf pipelines won't end reliance on Hormuz
stories.summary: Gulf producers could spend around $40 billion on pipelines that bypass the Strait of Hormuz, but even under the most aggressive diversification case about 2 million barrels a day would still pass through it in 2035, the International Energy Agency said in a report published 19 November. Roughly 7 million bpd of new bypass capacity is under construction or being considered, adding about $2 a barrel to Middle East export costs. Hormuz flows dropped from about 20 million bpd before the Iran war to about 3 million bpd in March-May; Saudi Arabia kept exports above 60% of prewar levels by rerouting crude to the Red Sea, though the IEA says its East-West pipeline expansion has not yet started. Qatar and the UAE have no feasible bypass for LNG, and Iranian strikes on Ras Laffan knocked out over 17 bcm of yearly capacity for about three years.
stories.market: The extra pipeline costs and stranded LNG capacity are relevant for Saudi Aramco, Gulf LNG exporters and tanker routes; the IEA also warned an end to the crisis could create a buyers' market with strong downward pressure on prices.

stories.headline: IMF lifts UAE 2026 growth forecast to 0.2% from a projected contraction
stories.summary: The IMF now expects the UAE economy to grow 0.2% in 2026, a sharp upgrade from its earlier forecast of a 3.9% contraction, after completing its Article IV mission on 18 November. It sees growth of 7.3% in 2027, slightly below its prior 7.7%. Hydrocarbon output is projected to rise 2.3% this year and 13.3% next, while non-oil activity shrinks 0.5% in 2026 before rebounding 5.4%. Inflation is forecast at about 5% this year, easing to about 3% in 2027. The Iran war, now in its ninth month, has hit tourism and aviation, but rerouted crude exports and strong buffers have cushioned the shock.
stories.market: The IMF called UAE banks resilient, with total assets above Dh5.8 trillion ($1.57 trillion) at end-September, which supports lenders listed in Abu Dhabi and Dubai; it flagged a cooling property market as a soft spot.

stories.headline: Bennett meets Netanyahu as Eisenkot races to form Israel's next government
stories.summary: Naftali Bennett held a meeting of two to three hours with caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at the Knesset on 18 November, delaying a summit of the opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot, whose spokesperson said he had not been told in advance. Eisenkot received the mandate to form a government on 8 November for 28 days, extendable by 14, but neither his 48-seat bloc nor Netanyahu's 53 seats reaches the 61 needed in the 120-member Knesset. Israeli TV reported Bennett urged a unity government with Eisenkot first in a rotation, while Liberman and Golan reject sitting with Netanyahu; Eisenkot's camp has opened talks with ultra-Orthodox parties. On Polymarket, the chance of Netanyahu leaving office by 31 December stood at 44.5%.
stories.market: Coalition clarity, and a government able to pass a budget, is the main domestic driver for the shekel and Tel Aviv-listed banks and insurers while the mandate clock runs into December.

stories.headline: South African inflation jumps to 5.2% on fuel, hours before the SARB decision
stories.summary: South Africa's consumer inflation rose to 5.2% in October from 4.5% in September, the highest in about two and a half years and slightly above the 5.1% consensus, Stats SA said on 18 November. Fuel prices rose 11.8% on the month and 42.9% on the year, with transport adding 2.1 percentage points to the headline rate, while food inflation was only 1.4%. Core inflation edged up to 4.2% from 4.0%, above the 4.0% forecast. The Reserve Bank, which raised the repo rate to 7.25% in September, announces its decision on Thursday 19 November around 13:00 GMT, and markets broadly expect a hold.
stories.market: The rand traded near 17.35 per dollar early on Thursday, close to its weakest level of the year, while the 2035 government bond yield was steady at 8.71%.

stories.headline: IMF strikes $2.3bn deal with Egypt as its loan programme nears the 15 December finish
stories.summary: The IMF reached a staff-level agreement with Egypt on Wednesday on the final reviews of its programmes, which would release about $2.3 billion if the board approves: roughly $1.5 billion under the Extended Fund Facility and up to $800 million from the Resilience and Sustainability Facility. That would bring total disbursements under both arrangements to about $9.6 billion before they expire on 15 December. Egypt beat its end-September targets for the primary surplus and tax revenue and has committed to a 5%-of-GDP primary surplus in 2026/27. Urban inflation slowed to 12.7% in October, after the central bank raised its overnight deposit rate by 100 basis points to 20%. President el-Sisi has said Egypt will not seek new IMF financing.
stories.market: The pound traded at about 53.75 per dollar on Tuesday, firmer than its record low of 56.39 in October but still about 13% weaker over the year; the deal supports Egyptian Eurobonds and local T-bill demand.

stories.headline: Naira slips to an 18-day low and reserves fall ahead of next week's CBN rate meeting
stories.summary: The naira weakened 0.55% to N1,363.23 per dollar on the official market on 18 November, its weakest in 18 days, while the parallel-market rate climbed to N1,460, widening the gap to about 7.1%. Foreign reserves fell by $500 million to $54.76 billion as of 17 November from an October peak of $55.26 billion, and weekly FX inflows dropped to $807.6 million from $2.48 billion. The central bank sold more than $3 billion into the market in October, yet the currency still lost ground that month. The Monetary Policy Committee meets on 23-24 November with the policy rate at 23% after a September cut; headline inflation eased to 14.06% in October and core to 10.78%, and all five analysts polled by Nairametrics expect a hold.
stories.market: Seasonal dollar demand is testing the CBN's firepower; a hold would favour naira carry trades in Treasury bills, while renewed FX pressure is a risk for Nigerian bank stocks and Eurobonds.

stories.headline: Taiwan stocks crash 4.4% below 40,000; regulator slashes short-selling limits
stories.summary: The Taiex plunged 1,768 points, or 4.4%, to 38,426.89 on Thursday 19 November, its seventh-largest points drop on record, after falling as much as 1,935 points intraday. TSMC lost 3.45% to NT$2,100, MediaTek 5.58% and UMC 5.16%, while memory makers Nanya and Winbond sank more than 9%; 20 stocks priced above NT$1,000 hit their daily limit-down. Foreign investors sold a net NT$24.3 billion, after NT$76.6 billion the day before, and the Taiwan dollar weakened to about 32.95 per US dollar, a more-than-19-month low. The Financial Supervisory Commission cut the intraday cap on short sales of borrowed shares from 30% to 3% of a stock's average daily volume, raised short-sale margin from 90% to 130%, and the Finance Ministry said its NT$500 billion stabilisation fund is ready to act. Triggers included the global AI-chip selloff, new US licence rules for advanced chip exports to Southeast Asia and Brazil, and bets on further Fed tightening.
stories.market: Taiwan's selloff is the sharpest gauge of the AI-hardware unwind: TSMC (2330.TW / TSM ADR), server makers and memory chips are most exposed, and the TWD slide adds to pressure on Asian EM currencies.

stories.headline: Kospi climbs 1.4% as Korea-China services deal lifts travel stocks
stories.summary: Seoul and Beijing reached a substantive conclusion to services and investment talks under their bilateral free-trade agreement, opening wider Chinese market access for Korean films, games and other businesses. Travel stocks jumped on Thursday 19 November: Hana Tour rose 16.75%, Jeju Air 11.47% and Korean Air 3.67%. The Kospi closed up 1.39% at 5,137.89, its second straight gain after a four-session slide, as SK hynix added 3.41% and Samsung Electronics 1.13%, even though foreigners were net sellers of 405 billion won. The won firmed 3 won to 1,330 per dollar and the three-year treasury yield fell 2 basis points to 3.72%.
stories.market: Korea's market diverged sharply from Taiwan's crash on the same day, with chip heavyweights SK hynix and Samsung holding up and China-exposed tourism and airline names leading.

stories.headline: Bank Indonesia hikes to 6% to defend a record-weak rupiah
stories.summary: Bank Indonesia raised its benchmark rate by 25 basis points to 6.00% on Wednesday 18 November, its first increase since June, and lifted the deposit and lending facility rates to 5.25% and 6.75%. The move follows the rupiah's slide to a record low on 12 November; it closed at Rp18,245 per dollar on Tuesday. Foreign investors pulled about $900 million from Indonesian stocks in the fourth quarter through 16 November, although overall net capital inflows reached $4.8 billion thanks to bond and sukuk issuance. Inflation eased to 3.23% in October and third-quarter GDP growth picked up to 5.47%. BI will also step up intervention in spot and forward markets and offer banks liquidity incentives from 1 December.
stories.market: The hike aims to keep Indonesian bond yields attractive versus a hawkish Fed; it supports the rupiah but tightens conditions for rate-sensitive banks and property names on the Jakarta Composite.

stories.headline: Malaysia's GDP beats estimate at 5.5% but ringgit hits near five-month low
stories.summary: Malaysia's economy grew 5.5% year on year in the third quarter, official data showed on 18 November, above the 5.3% advance estimate though slower than 6% in the second quarter. The ringgit still fell 0.64% to 4.1202 per dollar, its weakest since 26 June and one of its steepest daily drops since mid-June, as a hawkish US rate outlook weighed. The FBM KLCI slipped 0.53% to 1,566.73, dragged by consumer and plantation heavyweights such as Nestle and KL Kepong, while semiconductor names including Malaysian Pacific Industries and ViTrox gained.
stories.market: Ringgit weakness and lower oil prices are weighing on index heavyweights, while Malaysian chip-packaging stocks are trading against the regional AI-hardware selloff.

stories.headline: Philippine stocks inch off six-year low as peso stays near 63.7
stories.summary: The PSEi rose 0.20% to 5,511.84 on Wednesday 18 November, a second straight gain after Monday's six-year low, but decliners outnumbered advancers 106 to 55 and the broader All Shares index slipped. The peso weakened 4 centavos to P63.71 per dollar, after firming to P63.67 on Tuesday as oil prices eased towards 2.5-month lows. Traders cited stagflation worries, the risk of further US rate hikes, a prolonged domestic slowdown and uncertainty over the central bank's next move as reasons for caution.
stories.market: With the peso near record-weak territory and the BSP still in a tightening phase, banks have led the tentative rebound while property and mining shares lag.

stories.headline: Supreme Court orders poll body to probe fake voter-deletion claims in Delhi roll revision
stories.summary: A Supreme Court bench led by Chief Justice Surya Kant directed the Election Commission and Delhi's chief electoral officer to verify allegations that bogus Form 7 deletion requests were filed in Mustafabad constituency during the special intensive revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, and to act strictly in line with law if they are true. Congress leader Ali Mehdi's counsel said 36 of 37 applications examined were false, and Justice Joymalya Bagchi noted the Commission can blacklist booth-level agents who file fraudulent forms. About 47 lakh names were left off Delhi's draft roll from a pre-revision electorate of roughly 1.45 crore; claims and objections now close on 25 November and the final roll is due on 22 December. The same week the court heard related SIR pleas and a challenge by Eknath Shinde in the Shiv Sena dispute.
stories.market: No direct market impact; the SIR exercise is a running flashpoint between the government and opposition parties ahead of future state polls.

stories.headline: PM Tarique Rahman tells parliament reserves have climbed to about $36bn
stories.summary: Prime Minister Tarique Rahman told parliament on 18 November that Bangladesh's foreign-exchange reserves stood at around $36.35 billion as of 19 October, by his own calculation. That compares with $25.9 billion on 8 August 2024, according to Bangladesh Bank's weekly reserve measure, a rise of more than $10 billion since the interim period began. He was answering a question from a Chattogram MP in the closing sitting of the 13th Jatiya Sangsad's fourth session, which opened on 9 November.
stories.market: A thicker reserve buffer gives Bangladesh Bank more room to smooth the taka and service dollar debt, a key support for the country's external credit profile.
